correctness.rationale: For a witness outside T in the same row as a target, its omitted-neighbor set is the disjoint union of omitted cells in its row and column, so its row must have degree one and its column zero; the transposed condition is analogous. If a part has no empty line, the other must and the omitted cells form the corresponding nonsurjective transversal. With both kinds of empty lines, every incidence edge has a degree-one endpoint, so the graph is a star forest. One-sided centers give strictly fewer than q edges in this case. For a row-centered and a column-centered component, at least two stars and two isolates are required, giving at most p+q−4 edges; equality saturates both sides with exactly two components, opposite nontrivial centers, and one isolate each. At p=4 both bounds tie; outside the tie the larger bound determines the optimum. Inclusion–exclusion counts the nonsurjective maps, and each crossed-star configuration uniquely determines its two centers and two isolates. The families are disjoint. Independent direct adjacency tests of the optimum and next size ran on 2×2, 2×6, 3×3, 3×5, 4×4 and 5×5, matching all corresponding families and counts. Downward closure in T excludes larger complements when the next size is infeasible. Replay: python /workspace/review_checks/rook.py 2x2 2x6 3x3 3x5 4x4 5x5. The frozen output and code were inspected, not rerun; finite results corroborate, not replace, the proof.

This is coverage of mathematical content; it does not establish that the later-dated indexed record predates this record or settle priority.
residual_risks: Catalogue record dates do not decide priority. The finding's scientific overlap is based on the mathematical statements and proofs themselves.
